direct_answer:
BASF states it conducted a double materiality assessment for the first time in 2024 in accordance with the ESRS, building on prior assessments but with greater granularity and documentation, and intends to update it annually [Source 1]. The assessment was performed in three steps: (1) compiling a list of potential sustainability matters relevant to BASF’s business/customer industries and stakeholder groups, with particular attention to higher-risk business/value-chain areas; (2) using in-house experts and selected stakeholders (Nature Advisory Council and Human Rights Advisory Council) to identify and validate risks and opportunities linked to BASF’s impacts and dependencies, focusing on activities/sites/value-creation steps with elevated potential for negative impacts and risks; and drawing on BASF’s group-wide opportunity and risk management plus expert review to identify additional risks/opportunities; (3) after identifying material impacts/risks/opportunities, assigning each to ESRS topic/subtopic/sub-subtopic (per ESRS 1 AR 16), mapping applicable disclosure requirements and data points, and assessing “materiality of information” at disclosure/data-point level using EFRAG criteria (“decision-usefulness” and “stakeholder relevance”) [Source 1][Source 10]. Stakeholder interests were considered via direct inputs (Advisory Councils, BASF Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (big data analyses of customer and capital market interests) [Source 1]. Governance-wise, BASF reports that the Board of Executive Directors, Supervisory Board, Joint Works Council and Works Council Europe were informed about the process and outcome [Source 10].

BASF does not provide, in the retrieved passages, a consolidated list of sustainability matters that are material from both an impact and a financial perspective. It does state that: (i) Biodiversity and Ecosystems was defined as material as part of the 2024 double materiality assessment [Source 2]; (ii) topics in the category Own Workforce were defined as material [Source 3]; (iii) ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users was assessed as not material [Source 8]; and (iv) the opportunities and risks identified have financial effects affecting financial position/performance/cash flow, with financial effects in 2024 arising in connection with a risk identified in ESRS S3 Affected Communities [Source 8]. However, the passages do not explicitly identify which sustainability matters are material in both dimensions (impact and financial) as an output list [Source 8].
compliance_rationale: BASF describes a double materiality assessment process aligned to ESRS concepts (value-chain scope, identification of impacts/risks/opportunities, stakeholder inputs, linkage to risk management, mapping to ESRS topics, and data-point level materiality-of-information assessment) [Source 1][Source 10]. It also discloses some outcomes (e.g., Biodiversity and Ecosystems material; Own Workforce material; S4 not material; financial effects linked to an S3 risk) [Source 2][Source 3][Source 8]. However, the retrieved evidence does not include an explicit list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives, so the question cannot be fully answered from the provided passages [Source 8].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit identification of which sustainability matters are material from both an impact and a financial perspective (a clear ‘double-material’ output list) is not provided in the retrieved passages [Source 8].

Criteria/thresholds used to determine impact materiality (e.g., severity dimensions and likelihood) and financial materiality (likelihood/magnitude of financial effects) are not evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 1][Source 10].
Comprehensive results table of material matters across all ESRS topics (beyond the few examples cited) is not included in the retrieved passages [Source 2][Source 3][Source 8].

Stakeholder engagement limitations: for Biodiversity and Ecosystems, affected communities were not involved in identifying material topics; broader coverage of affected-stakeholder engagement across topics is not evidenced [Source 2].
key_findings: BASF conducted its first ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment in 2024, based on prior assessments but with increased granularity/documentation, and plans annual updates [Source 1].

Process included: compiling potential matters; expert and selected stakeholder validation of risks/opportunities tied to impacts/dependencies; focus on higher-risk value-chain areas; use of group-wide opportunity and risk management; expert review of impacts/dependencies [Source 1].
Stakeholder inputs included Advisory Councils/Civil Society Forum/multistakeholder networks and indirect big-data analysis of customer/capital market interests [Source 1].
Governance: key governing/employee representative bodies were informed of process and outcome [Source 10].

Biodiversity and Ecosystems was defined as material; BASF used stakeholder/literature, expert assessments, and digital/big data/AI tools (including BRF and IBAT) for this topic; affected communities were not involved for this cluster [Source 2].
Own Workforce topic category was defined as material [Source 3].
ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users was assessed as not material (B2B rationale) [Source 8].
BASF notes that identified opportunities/risks have financial effects; in 2024, financial effects arose linked to a risk under ESRS S3 Affected Communities [Source 8].
